deep.reconstruction:
Setting (Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, Ch. 12): p = 4q+1 is prime. Section 445 recaps the count of residues of fourth powers established on the previous pages. There are exactly q distinct biquadratic residues 1, α, β, γ, δ, ... ; this was proved first by the class (coset) argument of §§435-440 and again by the 'new' argument of §§441-444, where for each a ≤ 2q there is a unique b ≤ 2q with a^4 ≡ b^4, hence a^2+b^2 ≡ 0. The 3q nonresidues split into three classes of q elements each: I = {αx}, II = {αx^2}, III = {αx^3}, where x is a fixed nonresidue whose square x^2 is also a nonresidue.

§446. Every biquadratic residue α ≡ a^4 satisfies α^q ≡ a^{4q} = a^{p-1} ≡ 1 (mod p) by Fermat [this justification is mine; Euler just states it]. Question: do all nonresidues fail α^q ≡ 1?

§447. Let x^2 be a nonresidue; then x and x^3 are nonresidues too. Suppose x^{2q} ≡ 1. Then every αx^2 in class II satisfies (αx^2)^q = α^q x^{2q} ≡ 1. The residues α satisfy this as well. Together the residues and class II are 2q numbers, all of them squares; these are exactly all the quadratic residues 1^2, 2^2, ..., (2q)^2. So we would have y^q ≡ 1 for every quadratic residue y.

§448. Then n^{2q} ≡ 1 (mod p) for n = 1, ..., 2q. Since (p-n)^{2q} = n^{2q}, this holds for all n = 1, ..., 4q. So all differences among 1, 2^{2q}, ..., (2q)^{2q} would vanish mod p. Euler calls this absurd 'as shown above': an exponent 2q < p-1 cannot make every n^{2q} ≡ 1, by his earlier finite-difference argument that the 2q-th difference of n^{2q} is (2q)!, which is not ≡ 0 mod p.

§449. Hence x^{2q} ≢ 1. A fortiori:
- x^q ≢ 1, since x^q ≡ 1 would give x^{2q} ≡ 1.
- x^{3q} ≢ 1 [step mine: x^{3q} ≡ 1 together with x^{4q} ≡ 1 gives x^q ≡ 1].
Every nonresidue has the form αx^k with k = 1, 2, 3, and (αx^k)^q ≡ x^{kq} ≢ 1. Conclusion: a^q ≡ 1 (mod p) holds if and only if a is a biquadratic residue. This is the quartic analogue of Euler's criterion: a is a 4th-power residue mod p iff a^{(p-1)/4} ≡ 1.

§450. If a^q ≡ 1, then (a^k)^q ≡ 1, so every power of a is a biquadratic residue. Conversely, a nonresidue a has a^q ≢ 1.

§451. Take q odd, i.e. p ≡ 5 mod 8. Then (-1)^q - 1 = -2 ≢ 0, so -1 ≡ 4q is not a biquadratic residue. Also (-α)^q = -α^q ≡ -1, so all negatives p-α of residues are nonresidues.

§452. Hence for q odd there are no a^4 + b^4 ≡ 0 (mod p) [implicitly with p ∤ ab]: the residue of b^4 would be -α, which is impossible.

§453. Take q even, i.e. p ≡ 1 mod 8. Then (-1)^q = 1, so -1 is a biquadratic residue and the residue set is closed under negation.

§454. Thus for p ≡ 1 mod 8 and any a there is b with p | a^4 + b^4: take b^4 ≡ -a^4, which exists since -a^4 is a residue. Examples: p = 17, 41, 73, 89, 97. This prepares §455-456 on the next page: odd prime divisors of a^4+b^4 with gcd(a,b)=1 are ≡ 1 mod 8.
errors: §454: 'seu si 8q+1 sit numerus primus' reuses the letter q in a new sense. With q even, 4q+1 = 8(q/2)+1. The statement is right (p ≡ 1 mod 8) but the variable is silently renamed.
§§452/454: the condition that a and b are not divisible by p (or that the fourth powers are nonzero residues) is left implicit. Trivially p | a^4+b^4 when p divides both.

§447: the identification of residues ∪ class II with the set of all 2q quadratic residues is implicit. It rests on the earlier counts (q residues, q elements per class, all of them squares). This is correct but not restated.
§448 relies on an earlier result ('jam supra ostensum') that n^{2q} ≡ 1 cannot hold for all n when 2q < p-1. Valid, but imported from earlier.
§449: 'multo minus' for x^{3q} needs the small extra step x^{3q} ≡ 1 ⇒ x^q ≡ 1 (via x^{4q} ≡ 1). It is omitted but harmless.

results.what: For prime p=4q+1, a is a biquadratic (4th-power) residue iff a^q ≡ 1 mod p. Proved without primitive roots, via the coset/class structure and a finite-difference lemma.
results.modern_name: Euler's criterion for quartic residues (power-residue criterion a^{(p-1)/m} ≡ 1)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta, E262, 1761, and E449); general form systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones (1801), art. 106

results.what: Number of distinct biquadratic residues mod 4q+1 is q; the nonresidues fall into three cosets of size q
results.modern_name: Index of the subgroup of 4th powers in (Z/p)^* equals 4

results.what: -1 is a quartic residue mod p iff p ≡ 1 mod 8
results.usually_credited_to: Euler / classical (also Gauss's 1828 biquadratic residue memoir)

results.what: For p ≡ 5 mod 8 there is no a^4+b^4 ≡ 0 (p∤ab); for p ≡ 1 mod 8 every a admits b with p | a^4+b^4. Hence odd prime divisors of a^4+b^4 with gcd(a,b)=1 are ≡ 1 mod 8.
results.modern_name: Prime divisors of sums of two fourth powers (of x^4+1) are 2 or ≡ 1 mod 8
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (also Fermat-era observations); cyclotomic Φ_8 divisor theorem

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known Tractatus (E792, written c. 1750s, published 1849/1862). The quartic Euler criterion and the 8n+1 result on divisors of a^4+b^4 are standard and already attributed to Euler, e.g. E262 (1761). Only the primitive-root-free coset/difference proof style is mildly of interest, and even that is characteristic of Euler's known work.

checkable.sympy: all(set(pow(x,4,p) for x in range(1,p)) == set(a for a in range(1,p) if pow(a,(p-1)//4,p)==1) for p in primerange(5,2000) if p%4==1)
checkable.asserts: Quartic residues mod p=4q+1 are exactly the a with a^q ≡ 1 (§§446-450)

checkable.sympy: all(len(set(pow(x,4,p) for x in range(1,p))) == (p-1)//4 for p in primerange(5,2000) if p%4==1)
checkable.asserts: There are exactly q=(p-1)/4 distinct biquadratic residues (§445)

checkable.sympy: all(((p-1) in set(pow(x,4,p) for x in range(1,p))) == (p%8==1) for p in primerange(5,2000) if p%4==1)
checkable.asserts: -1 is a quartic residue iff q is even, i.e. p ≡ 1 mod 8 (§§451,453)

checkable.sympy: all(not any((pow(a,4,p)+pow(b,4,p))%p==0 for a in range(1,p) for b in range(1,p)) for p in primerange(5,300) if p%8==5)
checkable.asserts: For p ≡ 5 mod 8 no a^4+b^4 with p∤ab is divisible by p (§452)

checkable.sympy: all(all(any((pow(a,4,p)+pow(b,4,p))%p==0 for b in range(1,p)) for a in range(1,p)) for p in [17,41,73,89,97])
checkable.asserts: For 17,41,73,89,97 every a admits b with p | a^4+b^4 (§454)
Euler's example list is exactly the primes ≡ 1 mod 8 below 100

checkable.sympy: all(any(pow(n,2*((p-1)//4),p)!=1 for n in range(1,(p-1)//2+1)) for p in primerange(5,2000) if p%4==1)
checkable.asserts: Not all n^{2q} ≡ 1 for n ≤ 2q (the absurdity invoked in §448)
